intro: Every day the dice roll a premise and a dozen constraints, and the game has to honour all of them. Tonight's roll was seed 3301723394. Hear now the chronicle of each roll, and what the Alembic made of it.

rolls.became: The Alembic: the great glass still of the Archalchemist's tower, which saw him counterfeit gold and said so in court. The Marshals of the Hidden Road hid it that very night under a false moustache it never takes off. In each hideout it pretends to be something else that is also a pot: a teapot at the inn, a still among stills, a goblet in a hoard.

A witness may not write letters. Letters have handwriting, and handwriting gets you found. A teapot that posts buttons, though, is just a button shop. Every parcel goes out addressed to Nettle, postage due, and whoever opens the door pays a coin. That's the money.

The night it was taken, the Alembic had promised Nettle, the tower's apprentice, a coat's worth of buttons for her buttonless coat. An alembic drips. Now it drips buttons: tin in Little Hobbling, horn in Murkmere, gold on Mount Smoulder.
Tap the Alembic's card: it drips one button and posts it. The spouts you buy make heavier buttons, and postage is by weight, so a dripped button pays more and more.
A coat's worth of buttons. But how many is that, for an heroic coat? The frog tailor of Murkmere shrugs: 'Then all of them, I suppose.'

The Marshal's map is wrong on purpose, so nobody can trace the witness: the compass rose is labelled with days of the week, the river says Road, the east says HERE BE DRAGONS. Some parcels find a door and some find a ditch. Readings of the map (Tuesday Is North, Wring Out the Map, Ask the Dragon) are better guesses that send more parcels to a door. And because nobody can write back to a witness, the Alembic never learns how many reached her. Hence the face-down card, and hence it keeps posting, to be sure.
Nettle, the apprentice who swept the tower, wore a coat with no buttons, and was promised some. She lives in Nethermoor, which no honest map in this game shows until the very last reading.

rolls.value: distinct phases, each its own small economy
rolls.became: Three hideouts, three tarot cards. When a town has seen too many buttons, folk start to talk, and the Marshal deals the next card: a new cover, a new coin (pennies, wishbones, crowns), new helpers and new readings of a new corner of the bad map. The ledger comes along. The helpers and the leftover coin stay behind, because a forwarding address would lead straight to you.

Pigeons, postboys and parish carts; herons, ferry-toads and wisp lanterns; bats, griffins and Cousin Wyrm. At the 25th of a kind they count as a proper company and post twice as fast, and a red star goes up on the Post's card. Fifty: twice again.
The Post's great ledger has four digits, and so does the game: every button ever posted, up to 9,999.
About an hour and a half: three towns, a couple of hundred purchases, and helpers who keep posting (slowly) while you're away.
The whole game is a spread on a cloth: the Post, the hideout and the Map, each a card with a numeral and a title, with the past hideouts laid face up below them and one card face down in the corner.
Night-plum cloth, cream card faces, gold frames, and the rest of the 32 colours for tea cosies, fens and hoards.

A dub tune in G major: a deep bass that carries the hook, offbeat skanks with tape echo, a one-drop beat and a melodica that answers itself. The echo is the drip of the still. Every sound effect is in G major too, and the drip has its own little echo. The fen arrangement is the dubbiest, and the hoard is the fullest.
Told by the Chronicle, completely straight: 'And lo, the 25th pigeon joined, and the pigeons, being now a proper company, posted twice as fast.'
No calendar nod today. Just buttons.

rolls.value: the number hits its cap and the world crunches
rolls.became: At 9,999 the ledger has no fifth digit and can count no further. The world, which was only ever cards, crunches up like paper, and out of the ball rolls the one card that lay face down all game.

rolls.value: it was the wrong goal all along
rolls.became: The face-down card is Nettle's letter. It was a small coat. It takes six, and the first six came in the first week. The promise was never the coat. She only wanted to know the Alembic was safe, and every button said so. She kept them all, and gave the rest away: everyone in Nethermoor has buttons now.

outro: Sealed with a drip. Postage due.
